# Data Wrangling: Special Considerations with Survey Data

## Overview

Survey exports mix substantive responses with timestamps, progress indicators, timing variables, embedded metadata, and human-readable response labels. Treating that export as analysis-ready can lead to accidental inclusion of pilot cases or incorrect scoring.

In this example, we use the `qualtRics` package to import a Qualtrics export, separate logical groups of variables, and score the Ten-Item Personality Inventory (TIPI). The emphasis is on making each scoring decision explicit and inspectable.

## Load data

Read the survey, separate `StartDate` into date and time components, and flag pilot records. Keeping the `is_pilot_data` flag during preprocessing documents why rows were excluded.

```r
library(qualtRics)
library(tidyverse)

# set filename of survey file
fn = "data/demo_qualtrics_export.csv"

# filter out pilot data
PILOT_START_DATE = as.Date("2022-06-21")
qualtrics_df <- read_survey(fn) %>%
  separate(StartDate, into=c("dt_date", "dt_time"), sep=" ", remove=F) %>%
  mutate(is_pilot_data = dt_date < PILOT_START_DATE) %>%
  filter(!is_pilot_data) %>%
  mutate(participant_id = as.character(ResponseId))
```

## Split demographics into a separate dataset

Separating demographics creates a participant-level table that can be reviewed, protected, or shared under different rules from item-level response data. `ResponseId` remains as the linkage key.
```r
df_demo = qualtrics_df %>%
select(ResponseId, contains("demo"))

knitr::kable(df_demo)# %>% kableExtra::kable_paper(.)
```

## Split out survey metadata

Metadata such as duration and progress are useful for quality checks but are usually not substantive outcomes. Isolating them makes later inclusion decisions deliberate.
```r
df_metadata = qualtrics_df %>%
select(ResponseId, contains("Date"), contains("duration"), contains("progress"))

knitr::kable(df_metadata)# %>% kableExtra::kable_paper(.)
```

## Split timer data into a separate dataset

Page- or item-timing variables often have a different analytic grain than one-row-per-participant responses. A dedicated timing table prevents them from cluttering the main dataset.
```r
df_timings = qualtrics_df %>%
select(ResponseId, contains("timer"))

knitr::kable(df_timings)# %>% kableExtra::kable_paper(.)

```

## Score TIPI data

Scoring a scale is a sequence of transformations rather than one opaque command. We will reshape the items, convert labels to numbers, reverse the negatively keyed items, and then compute trait scores.

### Create reverse-scoring function

For a seven-point scale, reverse scoring maps 1 to 7, 2 to 6, and so on. Wrapping that rule in a function avoids copying slightly different recode statements for each item.

```r
reverse_code <- function(df, ques_label) {
  out_df = df %>%
    filter(tipi_question == ques_label) %>%
    mutate(response_n = recode(response, 
                               `Disagree strongly` = 7,
                               `Disagree moderately` = 6, 
                               `Disagree a little` = 5,
                               `Neither agree nor disagree` = 4,
                               `Agree a little` = 3, 
                               `Agree moderately` = 2,
                               `Agree strongly` = 1,
                               .default=-999))
  return(out_df)
}
```

### Separate TIPI data from main `qualtrics_df`

Selecting only TIPI columns narrows the working table to the variables needed for scoring while retaining the participant identifier.

```r
# create TIPI dataset -----
tipi_df = qualtrics_df %>%
  select(ResponseId, contains("TIPI"), -contains("_Timer"))
```

### Transform TIPI from wide to long

The wide export stores one item per column. Long form stores one item response per row, which makes it easier to apply the same recoding logic across questions.
```r
tipi_long = tipi_df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols=TIPI_1:TIPI_10, names_to="tipi_question", values_to="response")
```

### Recode values

Qualtrics exports descriptive labels. Converting them to the intended 1–7 scale is an analytic decision that should be visible in code rather than hidden in spreadsheet edits.
```r
tipi_long_r = tipi_long %>%
  mutate(response_n = recode(response, 
                             `Disagree strongly` = 1,
                             `Disagree moderately` = 2, 
                             `Disagree a little` = 3,
                             `Neither agree nor disagree` = 4,
                             `Agree a little` = 5, 
                             `Agree moderately` = 6,
                             `Agree strongly` = 7,
                             .default=-999))

```

### Apply Reverse Coding

NOTE: Extraversion: 1, 6R; Agreeableness: 2R, 7; Conscientiousness; 3, 8R; Emotional Stability: 4R, 9; Openness to Experiences: 5, 10R

The “R” marks negatively keyed items. Those items must be reversed before averaging; otherwise higher values would point in opposite directions within the same trait.

```r
tipi_long_recode2 = reverse_code(tipi_long_r, "TIPI_2")
tipi_long_recode4 = reverse_code(tipi_long_r, "TIPI_4")
tipi_long_recode6 = reverse_code(tipi_long_r, "TIPI_6")
tipi_long_recode8 = reverse_code(tipi_long_r, "TIPI_8")
tipi_long_recode10 = reverse_code(tipi_long_r, "TIPI_10")

tipi_long_nonrecoded = tipi_long_r %>%
  filter(tipi_question %in% c("TIPI_1","TIPI_3","TIPI_5","TIPI_7","TIPI_9"))

tipi_long_recode_all = bind_rows(tipi_long_nonrecoded,
                                 tipi_long_recode2,
                                 tipi_long_recode4,
                                 tipi_long_recode6,
                                 tipi_long_recode8,
                                 tipi_long_recode10)
```

### Finally transform to wide format

Returning to one row per participant makes the scored traits convenient to join with demographics, outcomes, or experimental conditions. Inspect both the recoded items and final scale scores before discarding intermediate objects.

```r
tipi_wide_recoded = tipi_long_recode_all %>%
  select(-response) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from="tipi_question", values_from="response_n") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(tipi_extraversion = mean(c(TIPI_1, TIPI_6), na.rm=T)) %>%
  mutate(tipi_agreeableness = mean(c(TIPI_2, TIPI_7), na.rm=T),
         tipi_conscientiousness = mean(c(TIPI_3, TIPI_8), na.rm=T),
         tipi_emostability = mean(c(TIPI_4, TIPI_9), na.rm=T),
         tipi_openexperience = mean(c(TIPI_5, TIPI_10), na.rm=T))

knitr::kable(tipi_wide_recoded %>% select(contains("TIPI_", ignore.case = F)))# %>% kableExtra::kable_paper(.)

knitr::kable(tipi_wide_recoded %>% select(contains("tipi_", ignore.case = F)))# %>% kableExtra::kable_paper(.)
```

## Takeaways

Reliable survey preprocessing preserves identifiers, distinguishes metadata from responses, documents exclusions, and makes scoring rules explicit. Intermediate long-form data are valuable audit artifacts even when the final analysis table is wide.
